messages.subject: Re: Problem with generating MSImageSet object
messages.body_plain:
Hi Purva,

You don't want to use generateImage(), which is actually the function for generating *simulated* data. The first argument of generateImage() is actually meant to be a pattern of regions to simulate, so you're telling to R to simulate images with probably thousands of distinct regions, which is why it's taking so long.

How did you load "intensityData"? Where did it come from?

The usual way of using your data in Cardinal is to use the readMSIData() function to read your data from an imzML or Analyze file, such as:

mydata <- readMSIData("path/to/file.imzML")

If you loaded your data another way, such as reading it from a text file, you need to use the MSImageSet function to turn it into an MSImageSet:

mydata <- MSImageSet(spectra=intensityData, mz=mzData, coord=coordData)

where you have presumably read "intensityData", "mzData", and "coordData" into R some other way.

Please see ?readMSIData and ?MSImageSet for details on loading your data, or creating an MSImageSet from data you've loaded.

-Kylie

messages.subject: Inquiry on References/Details about Pre-processing
messages.body_plain:
Hello Kylie,

I am learning details about the pre-processing steps given in Section 4 of the document Cardinal: Analytic tools for mass spectrometry imaging <https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/Cardinal/inst/doc/Cardinal-walkthrough.pdf>, in order to make suggestions to my biologist collaborators on different specific methods in real MALDI data analysis.  With mainly background from statistics, I am now in the search of literature about the details of the implementation.  Hence, I would like to ask for general additional resources, comments, and/or suggestions.

The following are the references I identified, with relevant key words following the titles.
> Alexandrov (2012) - MALDI imaging mass spectrometry - statistical data analysis and current computational challenges (general introduction)
> Alexandrov and Kobarg (2011) - Efficient spatial segmentation of large imaging mass spectrometry datasets with spatially aware clustering (peak alignment)
> Alexandrov et al (2010) - Spatial segmentation of imaging mass spectrometry data with edge-preserving image denoising and clustering (peak picking, peak alignment)
> Deininger et al (2011) - Normalization in MALDI-TOF imaging datasets of proteins - practical considerations (normalization)
> Yang, He, and Yu (2009) - Comparison of public peak detection algorithms for MALDI mass spectrometry data analysis (smoothing, baseline reduction, peak picking)

In particular, I would like to know the references for these pre-processing steps: peak filtering and data reduction (for example, how does the reference spectrum work for the pig fetus dataset from CardinalWorkflows).

Pardon me for this introductory-level inquiry.  Thank you!

Best regards,
Yumin

messages.subject: Re: Inquiry on References/Details about Pre-processing
messages.body_plain:
I apologize for taking some time to get back to you.

Without a reference, the peak alignment method will generate a reference from the local maxima of the mean spectrum. Peaks are then aligned to the nearest local maximum in the mean spectrum (within a certain tolerance given in either absolute m/z units or relative ppm units). This is similar (but may not be identical to) the described method in the Alexandrov publications of "moving peaks 'uphill' the mean spectrum".

The default peak filtering method simply applies the rule described in the Alexandrov publications of selecting only those peaks which occur in XX% of considered spectra. In Alexandrov & Kobarg (2011) they only use peaks which occur in 1% of considered spectra, which is the default setting.

The data reduction step with method="peaks" simply goes back through all of the spectra, and reduces the dataset to the reference m/z. This is done by finding the limits of the peaks for each spectrum (by finding the nearest local minima on either side of each peak), and then either taking the max intensity (height) in those limits, or taking the area under the curve "area" as the intensity value for that peak. I have no paper reference for this since it is simply grabbing the desired peaks in each spectrum.

I hope this helps.

-Kylie
